newsitem.title: USA: U.S. factory orders down more than expected in May.
newsitem.headline: U.S. factory orders down more than expected in May.

text.p: Weak demand for new cars and airplanes helped push the value of new orders to U.S. factories down more sharply than anticipated during May, the Commerce Department said on Wednesday.

Orders fell 0.7 percent to a seasonally adjusted $323.3 billion -- the second drop in the past three months -- after a revised 1.4 percent increase in April orders and a 1.7 percent decline in March. Wall Street economists had forecast only a 0.2 percent falloff in May orders.
Shipments and order backlogs also weakened from April.
The report added to signs that factory business was tapering off in the second quarter, a development that analysts had forecast on the basis of weaker retail sales.
On Tuesday, for example, Chrysler Corp. reported that its overall sales of new vehicles weakened for a fifth straight month in June.
Orders for all types of durable goods, from cars to turbines, fell 0.7 percent to $175.9 billion in May after a 1.8 percent April increase.
Orders for nondurables like food and paper products also were down, declining 0.7 percent in May to $147.5 billion after a 0.8 percent rise in April.
Among key categories, transportation equipment orders declined 3 percent to $38.5 billion following a 2.8 percent rise in April.
Excluding transportation, factory orders were down 0.4 percent in May following a 1.2 percent rise in April.
Previously, the department said that factory orders rose 1.2 percent in April, but it revised that up moderately.
There are other signs of easing in manufacturing activity.

On Tuesday, the National Association of Manufacturers said its June index of activity fell to 55.7 from 57.1 in May as new orders and production each grew more slowly. Any reading over 50 indicates an expanding manufacturing economy, though the pace was less robust last month than earlier in the year.
Total shipments of manufactured goods, which reflect more immediate demand than orders, decreased by 1 percent in May to $323.5 billion after a 1.2 percent increase in April.
Defence contractors' orders, which are subject to wide monthly swings, plunged 13 percent to $5.5 billion in May after a 27.5 percent jump in April.
Orders for non-defence capital goods, a measure of business' expansion plans, rose 0.4 percent to $43.9 billion in May after declining 1.7 percent in April.
During May, order backlogs were virtually unchanged at $522 billion after two straight monthly drops of 0.3 percent in both March and April.
Inventories of finished goods rose 0.4 percent in May to $443.3 billion after increasing 0.7 percent in April.

The department said that inventories have risen in 10 of the past 11 months, potentially signalling that factories may need to scale back production in the future to avoid having excess stocks on hand.
